articles.title: HEARING THE GOSPEL FOR THE FIRST TIME
articles.author: W. Dickson

paragraphs.text: The persons to whom these preachings were addressed had never heard the gospel before. It was the first time they had heard the gospel, and I would like to preach, with God’s help, from that standpoint tonight. I do not want to preach to you as having heard the gospel a hundred times, a thousand times; I want to preach to you tonight as if you had never heard the gospel before, which will, of course, mean raising some very simple questions. The raising of them may probe your conscience; it may cause you to question the understanding you have of God’s thoughts towards you in grace, as to whether by faith you have taken them up for yourself. We are living in serious times and the very foundations are being sapped. Children go to school and the very things they are taught in the homes of their parents are undermined, are questioned; they are told they are fables. What will help them? The only thing that will help them will be an absolute conviction in their own hearts, as having had to do with a personal Saviour, and that they trust in Him with regard to His finished work, and so have present peace and an assured hope for the future.

Here was this man in Acts 8; he was reading his Bible and as he read it he would ask the question, ‘Why would it be necessary for this Man to die? This Person who underwent such sufferings, why was it necessary?’ Is everyone in this room convicted as to why the death of Jesus was necessary? Are you among those who would say,

‘Would it not have been a happier state of things if, instead of the death of Jesus, God had, in His own sovereign grace and mercy, decided to save every person, no matter what the sinful state, without calling upon them to repent and to make acknowledgment of the need of a Saviour?’ There are thousands of people in this world tonight who think that way; who think it would be much happier if, so to speak, God had wiped the slate clean and just taken every man, woman, and child into relationship with Himself.

Why was the death of Jesus necessary? You young people, just ponder that question, think it over. O, beloved, the God that we have to do with has a throne of righteousness, of infinite majesty, and holiness; that throne was sinned against by man, which brought in its train a terrible heritage of death and sorrow; and while God loved His creature with a heart so great, so wonderful human minds could never penetrate the depth of the heart of God—yet the majesty, the honour, the righteousness of that throne stood out in the face of the universe as having been impugned and challenged by sin. How could God take into relationship with Himself every human creature without raising with them how they stood in regard to the claims of that throne? That was why Jesus died.

You say, ‘I thought He died for me’. Indeed He died for you, but, first of all, He died to meet the righteous claims of that holy throne of God, which had been impugned by sin, that God’s heart might come out in all its blessedness and all its compassion—
‘The river of His grace;
Through righteousness supplied,
Is flowing o’er the barren place
Where Jesus died’. (Hymn 13)

O, beloved hearer, that is why He died. That is why that holy, sinless, spotless life, so pleasing, so delightful to the heart of God, was given up; it was in order that the claims of the righteousness of God might be met and a basis provided whereby you and I, as guilty sinners, in simple faith might draw nigh and take full advantage of that work, and, in virtue of it, stand before a holy God with not one single charge against us.

Have you ever let that basic truth sink deep into your heart? Have you ever sat down and said to yourself, ‘Without the death of Jesus my need would never have been met; without the death of Jesus I would for ever have been shut out from all that favour and blessing and joy that is in the presence of God; without the death of Jesus it would never have been mine’?

Do you wonder that this man in Acts 8 went on his way rejoicing? I do not. It was the first time he had heard the gospel, the first time he had heard the good news, the first time he had heard that great evangelist, Philip. Oh what a preacher Philip must have been; I would love to have heard Philip preach; not only to hear the words that he used but to see the spirit in which he would speak tenderly of Jesus. The eunuch says in effect, ‘Why should I remain here in this world that crucified Jesus?’—and he went down into the water of baptism and went on his way rejoicing. Are you rejoicing? Are you going on your way rejoicing? There is no testimony so great as a happy christian. No preaching like a happy christian. Beloved George Herbert used to say, ‘I would rather see a sermon than listen to one any day’. When you go to the office, do they see a sermon? In saying this it is, of course, important to remember that practical salvation is connected with the confession of the Lord’s name. As this eunuch went up to that queen’s palace, he would say, ‘I went down into that water of baptism and identified myself with Jesus in His death and I have no place here; my joy, my life, is to testify for that Saviour and to live for Him here; even in the queen’s palace I can testify and live for Jesus’.

In Acts 16 we have this gaoler. He had never heard the preaching before, at least so far as we know; it is very unlikely that he had; but God in His ordering had placed him in touch with these two men, Paul and Silas, in the prison, and God came into his circumstances in His wonderful mercy, making him feel the need of salvation, and Paul preached this short sermon in answer to the man’s request, “What must I do that I may be saved?” Have all present asked that question? Now let us go back in our history. Can you recall the day when you said,

‘What must I do to be saved’? I believe in conversion; I believe in a revolution in souls as affected by the grace of God that will effect an about-turn, an about-face; instead of facing towards the world you face towards Christ, you face towards God. Here was this man and he uttered that cry, “What must I do that I may be saved?” Would it go without an answer? No, I do not think so. I do not think heaven would allow a cry like that to go unanswered.

Oh, if anybody in this room tonight is in any sense not in the gain of the gospel, not in the gain of salvation, will you not utter that cry tonight—‘What must I do to be saved’? From the world? Yes, salvation from the world; salvation from sin; salvation from the flesh. ‘What must I do to be saved?’ O what a cry! “Believe on the Lord Jesus and thou shalt he saved”. It is not only the death of Jesus, but “Believe on the Lord Jesus and thou shalt be saved”—a glorious, living Man there in the presence of God; your Priest, your Advocate, your Saviour, your Lord, your Friend, your Shepherd, your eternal hope—
‘O what a Saviour is Jesus the Lord!

Well may His Name by His saints be adored!’ (Hymn 169)—a Person so glorious, so available to you in all your need. “Believe on the Lord Jesus and thou shalt be saved, thou and thy house”—and thy house; what a promise! It means, in effect, that everything about you circumstantially will come under the blessed rays of God’s grace, and what a transformation it will be!

O, you young people, I would again impress upon you the simplicity of calling upon the Lord’s name, just turning to the Lord and calling upon Him. There is nothing like it in any circumstance in which you find yourself, whether it be an inward thing or an outward thing; whether it is a sin that besets you inwardly or a tie, an association, or some friendship that you find it difficult to break; its cords have got you tightly and you long to break it; you feel it is sapping your spiritual life away; you feel it is not honouring to the Lord that you should continue in it—“Believe on the Lord Jesus and thou shalt be saved”! Confess His name and prove the power of it; such power comes into your soul if you take that name upon your lips and cling to Jesus as the living Man up there available to you.

In Acts 17 these people had never heard the gospel before. It must have been quite a test to preach at Athens. These philosophers were questioning Paul about his gospel. These men were all agnostics, and there are more agnostics in the world than there are infidels or atheists. An agnostic is a person who will say, ‘Yes, we know there is a God, but it is not within human capability to be certain as to how He can be approached’.

That is an agnostic. Do you think like that? Has the light of the revelation of God in Jesus not affected you? “To the unknown God”—that is how their altar was dedicated. You could not say that, could you? Could any in this room say that?—“To the unknown God”—surely not!
Paul’s spirit was painfully excited in him and he started to preach to them about the resurrection of Jesus.

Again I want to speak very simply. Is everybody in this room, from the youngest to the oldest, convicted as to the resurrection of Christ? You say, It is unnecessary to raise a question like that. It is not. I have known persons forsake the truth and, when asked why they were taking that road, they said they did not believe in the resurrection of Jesus; they found it impossible to grasp with their natural minds the fact that Jesus was raised from the dead. You will not grasp it with your mind in any case, you will only grasp it by faith! Think of this, young people! Think of this, because if you have the light of a risen and glorified Christ in your soul it will give you conviction and a power that nothing will be able to shake. Paul said that God has given testimony of the fact that He is going to judge the world in righteousness by that Man in having raised Him from the dead. These are great basic matters; Paul devotes the whole of 1 Corinthians 15 to this great matter of the resurrection of Christ, because “if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain”. You have no basis for justification, no basis for acceptance in the presence of God, no basis for hope, apart from the resurrection of Christ.

These cults that come into colleges and offices, with all their strange teachings, seek to affect young believers. What is your safeguard? Absolute conviction that God raised Jesus from the dead, and that that Man is your Saviour, and that you have a present living link with Him by faith.

In Acts 26 you find another man who had never heard the gospel before, a king. He was sitting on a throne with Bernice amidst all the pomp, and Paul—a happy christian—preaches the gospel to him. I have often been very, very interested as to the character of the preaching of Paul to king Agrippa in these verses we read, as to why Paul preached the gospel in this particular way to him. It was quite remarkable to speak to a heathen king, who had never heard the gospel before, about an “inheritance among them that are sanctified”. What was he meaning? Oh I think I know what he was meaning! What, in effect, he was telling king Agrippa was—‘I know something of the glory of God and the great thoughts of God in purpose and blessing, and were you to give me your throne and your kingdom it cannot match what God has given me—an inheritance among the sanctified’. Do you feel that way, young people? If the world was to offer its best to you tonight, its very best, if it was to offer you fame, honour, and wealth tonight, has the Spirit of God so wrought with you that you would say, ‘My place amongst the people of God is greater than all’. Would you say that?

Agrippa would say, ‘That man there, looking up at me, that man has more than I have, a thousand times more. That man there is preaching to me, and me a king, and he is telling me that he has an inheritance among those that are sanctified’. The historians tell us that his link with Bernice, by his side, was an immoral one, and there was a man preaching about an inheritance “among them that are sanctified”, sanctified, and Agrippa’s whole life was in need of the cleansing power of the blood of Jesus. What an arrow to his conscience!

May these words come to you tonight as if it were the first time in your life that you had heard the gospel. There are some days, some nights, when persons get a convicting touch; they have gone on for a long time until the Spirit of God meets them in their souls with a convicting touch. Agrippa acknowledged to Paul that he was almost persuaded to become a christian. Almost—you remember the hymn, ‘Almost persuaded’? Oh how many have been almost persuaded. Are you among them tonight?

Almost persuaded? Or are you going to say tonight, I am fully persuaded “that he is able to keep for that day the deposit I have entrusted to him”, 2 Timothy 1: 12. I trust that these basic truths will affect your heart and give you to see the reality and power of the gospel, that it is no myth but is founded on the Scriptures and centred in the living Person at the right hand of God. May you be drawn to Him tonight, every one of you, for His name’s sake.

I was just attracted, beloved brethren—perhaps because in a way it suited me—by the reference in our hymn at the beginning to ‘love’s resting place’, just to linger on the words as we sang them, as we have sung them I suppose countless times. But sometimes something you are very familiar with touches you, perhaps because you have a need of it, and perhaps we all have a need of it—that is, love’s resting place. There is the

turmoil in the world, indeed in the country, to which our beloved brother referred, circumstances which exist as to which men, and for that matter women, scarcely seem to know any solution. I wonder sometimes how we think of these things, whether we think of these public situations as to how they might affect us. The great thing is, not how they affect us circumstantially but how they affect us in our spirits and souls—the general disorder and lawlessness and how God must view it and over against that I think the saints need a resting place.

Of course there are other circumstances; there are our beloved sisters in hospitals and in homes in the city at the present time who would remind us of the need for love’s resting place, and as you speak perhaps with one and another of them you are impressed with how needed it is. I think the Lord has something special to say to us in the city (not that I can say what it is) in our having so many sisters laid aside at the present time. Perhaps it is to increase the development of tenderness amongst us. It must be for something, and I suggest that it could at least be for that. Then there is the ordinary weariness of the way, where one gets tired, and things like that accumulate, and again one looks for a resting place. I have referred to these scriptures because that is what they suggest to me, in fact in one it is explicit.

The place where we need a resting place is, of course, the wilderness. We shall rest when we are with Christ, although it is interesting that Paul does not refer to rest, as far as I recall, in relation to the rapture, but in relation to the appearing—“repose with us, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven”, 2 Thessalonians 1: 7. But this is the place where we need rest, and we need not a resting place that we have worked out or chosen for ourselves; what we need is love’s resting place. “And they came to Elim”; it just says that, “they came to Elim”. There was no special guidance or direction, though I suppose that they had divine direction at this point, because there was the cloud. “They came to Elim”. It is just as if in our circumstances the Lord allows us to come, almost unexpectedly, to where we may find what we quickly recognise, not as something that has just happened, but as being love’s resting place for the moment, and just what we need is there. There are the springs of water and the palm trees, which have often been applied in relation to the availability of the Spirit and of the saints, as providing love’s resting place; but we just come to it. It is not that we sought it out, we just came to it, and it is a great thing, beloved, in our circumstances to recognise the moment when love has given us a resting place that we did not expect.

Then the thing is, if I could just put it simply, to make the best of it and make the most of it, and enjoy it. One day we will have to journey from it, as the next chapter shows, but for the moment, if we touch love’s resting place, just providentially on the way, let us enjoy it, let us recuperate there, let us find what Jesus promised in Matthew 11: 30, rest to our souls, because that is what most of us I suppose need a good deal of the time. Most of the time we are under some kind of stress; for the minor part of the time we are at rest, I expect everybody is like that. For a lot of the time we are in the turmoil, for a little of the time we are at rest, but how blessed the rest is; and we just came to it.

But then in Numbers 10 we did not just come to it, it was sought out for us. “The ark ..: went before them in the three days’ journey, to search out a resting-place for them”, and if it is the ark, that is Christ, that searches out a resting place for us in the wilderness, then it must be love’s resting place. That is to say, it is a place where it can rest—it says, “when it rested”, a place where Christ Himself, in relation with His saints in the wilderness, can find a resting place—and where He can rest and we can rest. In a sense He has no rest here. “My Father worketh hitherto and I work” (John 5: 17), and the work goes on. He had, when He was here, no place where He could lay His head. Strikingly enough, He had that rest in the ship in the storm, but otherwise very, very little rest. He was weary with the way He had come (John 4: 6), but even for Him I think that He found love’s resting place in the Father’s work in relation to the woman who came out that she might draw water.

Beloved, the Lord searches out a resting place for us, and therefore if we find a need for rest the thing is not to look for rest but to look for the Lord, and to seek to discover in our spirits and under the guidance of the Holy Spirit just the way in which He is going, where He is going to rest, as Mr. Darby has the expression in his letter to the Irish clergy, ‘casual rest is of the supreme mercy’ (Coll. Wrtgs. Vol. 1, p.9). But beloved, if the Ark sought it out, then we may safely rest there, because when it sets forward it deals with the enemies, puts them all down, scatters them, in order that when it rests the people of God may rest. The Lord would give us, as I say, rest to our souls. If you reflect on the Scriptures you will notice very much how the question of rest enters into them, in a positive way too, and as valuable, and it should be so for us, because the Lord will provide it for us. He will search out a resting place for us, as much as to say, ‘It will not be here, and it will not be there’; you may have thought it was!
‘You will not find rest in this or that, but I have a rest’; and the Lord is going before us in the wilderness and would bring us to a place where we can rest, because He can rest.

Beloved, as I say again, the thing is, when we are under any kind of pressure or strain, or just with the ordinary weariness of everyday life (it affects some of us at different times, and affects all of us in different ways) not for me to search for a rest but to follow the Lord and the Lord will bring us to a resting place which He has searched out. It may be just for a moment, because if you look at Numbers 33 you find it was all movement, and one place after another; but if the ark had sought out the movements in each place, whether it was just for a day or a night, or for a week or a month, or whatever period, if the ark stopped there then that was a place where you could rest. I expect what most of us need is rest to our souls.
There is a need for rest in body, but there is a need for rest to our souls, and what the Lord Himself seeks out is a place where we may safely rest, and as I say again, it is love’s resting place.

I suggest that John found that, John knew that. John records the controversy and strife that entered into the Lord’s blessed life here, and in what he portrays in his gospel how much conflict and exercise there is. In the fifth chapter and the eighth chapter, how much conflict and strife there is with those who are opposed to Him; but there was a disciple whom Jesus loved who could lean at supper on His breast. That is to say, he found love’s resting place, and the striking thing in chapter 13 is that he found it in a moment when Jesus Himself was troubled in spirit. Think of that! The question of the betrayer arose there; their feet had been washed and Jesus had taken His garments again, and He was leaving the world to go to the

Father, and all that phase of things was over in relation to the disciples, and then our mind is concentrated for a few moments on the betrayer, the one who would deliver Him up, and Jesus was troubled in spirit; but even at that moment there was still love’s resting place.

John could lean on His breast then—indeed this is quoted in effect from chapter 13—in circumstances like that, when Jesus was troubled, and yet He would still provide a rest for a disciple whom He loved. Beloved, I need not say in relation to all the saints that He loves them all, and He would provide this kind of rest for them all. It just comes back to what I was saying a moment ago, that if we seek for rest the thing is to find the Lord, and then having found the Lord to get sufficiently near Him that you can take up this place. There is a sense in which it is special to John, but then there is a sense in which we may perhaps appropriate it for ourselves in our spirits, that there is a resting place in which, I think I could safely say, He Himself is content to have us in love’s resting place.

Well, beloved, I refer to these things because these familiar hymns sometimes strike a new chord in your mind. I suppose most of us speak here on a Tuesday night in relation to some impression that we have had ourselves, that has been formed in us out of our own experience and can be communicated to the saints, and the Lord would I think touch us all with a sense of the rest that He would give us. In the Song it says, “On my bed, in the nights, I sought him whom my soul loveth” (Song of Songs 3: 1), and He came and she was at rest when He came; not before and not apart from Him, nor may we be beloved; we cannot be at rest apart from Him. But in our circumstances He will provide for us what we do not expect. He will search things out and make Himself available, in order that we ourselves may find in Him love’s resting place. Well, may it be so, and may I say, may it do us good, for His name’s sake.

My desire is to say a word about “the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof!” The chariot of Israel must involve great movement in the testimony. We do well to stick closely to the actual words of Scripture because, despite the pictures in books about Elijah’s going up into heaven, he never went up in the chariot of fire. Jehovah would take him up “by a whirlwind”; that is rapture! Philip the evangelist had a similar experience when the Spirit of the Lord caught him away from his convert, and he was found many miles away in a different place altogether. A whirlwind can do that; how much more the Spirit of God! When we go up, beloved, at the assembling shout of Christ, it will be the power of the Spirit that will be in operation. You think of the resurrection of Jesus—the Father raised Him, He raised Himself, and was “made alive in the Spirit”, 1 Peter 3: 18. What power there was when Christ was raised and was glorified by ascending into heaven! But Elijah’s experience was remarkable; the only man, apart from Jesus, to go up in such a way. Moses died, but Elijah did not die. He was carried up by a whirlwind into the heavens.

My point today, for the encouragement of my heart and the hearts of the brethren, is that the chariot of Israel is still here, and the testimony is going on to a triumphant conclusion. Let no one think that things are going to peter out; they are not. We do not despise the day of small things, because the greatest event is about to happen, and it will not happen as the result of a nuclear explosion. Let the brethren’s hearts be stabilised, especially those of the young people. It was said in the last war that the assembly is not going to be bombed into heaven, nor will she be. The Lord will see to that. Think of the intrinsic value of the assembly to the heart of Christ! She is going to go up in her own dignity. She will come down again to the renewed earth in her own dignity. But Elijah was going to be taken up because God loved him so. You say, ‘Did he not fail?’; but what servant has not failed?—except the Servant of servants, Christ Himself.

But Elijah was loved by heaven. So he goes over this ground, and it is very sad ground to go over, because in all these places that he visits sin had come in, and the transgressions of the people of God were found there. Think of the beginning, Gilgal. Elijah knew what that was—the condemnation of the flesh, in me and in us all; Gilgal, the place where God removed the stink of the world from us. We are not to be like it, beloved. Remember that word we had this afternoon—“Let the filthy make himself filthy still”, Revelation 22: 11. We are to be righteous still, and holy still. But Gilgal, the place of the rolling away of the reproach of this world from the people of God, what had it become? Amos 4: 4 will tell you what it had become—multiplying transgressions at Gilgal, and they had made it a place of sacrifice to demons. This is what, alas, has happened in the history of christendom. Directly after the apostles’ time the moral collapse came in.

Then Bethel; you say, the house of God, where Jacob found himself once in the presence of a God who insisted on blessing him in spite of all that Jacob was. He said, “This is ... the house of God”, and so he named it; and I have found, beloved, in that same house, that in spite of all that I am and all that I have done, God has sovereignly and graciously blessed. He is doing it all around us, in this room, today. He is intent upon blessing. And yet, what had Bethel become? You read Amos 7! Amos says, “I was no prophet”. There was no official hierarchy, no enthronement in a cathedral, for Amos—a herdman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit. The priest (Amos 7: 12, 13) said to him, You, Amos, prophesy no more in Bethel; it is the king’s sanctuary, and the house of the kingdom. We do not want the word of God. Also in Amos, Bethel is said (see Amos 4: 4) to transgress. So these are places that had gone wrong that were being visited by the prophet Elijah for the last time. Let us take heed, beloved. The word of God will not always be found in this scene. There will come a time of famine—not of thirst for water, nor hunger for bread, but a famine of hearing the word of God (see Amos 8: 11). They will run to and fro and not find it.

So they go to Jericho, the place of the overthrow of this world, at the very entrance to the land of blessing. What had happened at Jericho? Already in the book of Kings Jericho had been rebuilt in the lawlessness of man. God had said that Jericho was never to be rebuilt, but man says, I want a nice religious world, so I will rebuild it myself. God says, You will do it in the death of your first-born, if you do it (Joshua 6: 26), and so it came about (1 Kings 16: 34).

Jericho, that wicked city, had been built again, and Elijah, pays it a visit, but he does not stay there. He says, “Jehovah has sent me to the Jordan”. What was the Jordan? The confines of the land, and Elijah was going right outside the profession at that time. Some of us have had to have heart-rending experiences in leaving where the whole truth, as it is in Jesus, is not held, though there are believers there; there were believers in Israel when Elijah was doing this journey with Elisha. The two of them went on and talked. I love that. It opens the door for the delightful experiences that we have together over the Scriptures in reading meetings, conversation together one with another.

They two went on and talked. How near heaven was as those two men talked together! Then the chariot of Israel parts them—the one man going up to heaven without dying, the other man left here to bear the testimony of grace so long as God pleased to continue.

Elisha would like that. The Syrians were the great enemy of Israel. A type of the king of the north was the Syrian to Israel, and always a persecutor. But do you know what grace does with persecutors? An army was invading Israel, and Elisha says to Jehovah, “Smite this nation, I pray thee, with blindness”. God did it. That might seem severe, but wait! They were after Elisha, to put him to death, to rid Israel of the word of God. But it was not to be, and hence they were smitten with blindness. Elisha said to them, “Follow me, and I will bring you to the man whom ye seek”. He led them right into the middle of Samaria. The king of Israel said, “My father, shall I smite? Shall I smite them?” Elisha says, No; you give them bread and water. He prayed again, and their eyes were opened and they found themselves in the presence of divine grace. That is where I found myself, and I do not want to be anywhere else, held in the pursuit of the testimony, but in the spirit of grace. So that wonderful scene ends, but there is still the chariot of Israel and the horsemen.

In chapter 13 we have king Joash—he was not a good king either—but he did get the words of Elisha right, because he repeats them. Elisha himself is leaving this scene. What is going to happen now? I would remind the brethren that, when Mr. Darby lay dying, Mr. Champney, his heart full of foreboding for the future without Mr. Darby, said to him, ‘O, Mr. Darby, what of the future?’ The dying man replied, ‘There is no future for the christian but glory!’

How magnificent that is! It meant that the chariot of Israel was still going on. We are not yet at the end, but we are very near it. Beloved, this occasion is to strengthen the brethren in this city and wherever brethren are walking in the truth and representing it in their own places.

They are to go on “firm, immovable, abounding always in the work of the Lord”, 1 Corinthians 15: 58. There is no denying the power in the testimony! You say, ‘Things are very broken, and humbling and weak’. I say, The chariot of Israel is still going on.

We do not want to be like this man—smiting three times only. It is not enough, beloved! We have to put all that we have into the testimony at the present time. Think of the power that could be exerted with all of us, young and old, holding forth the word of life. So it is “an arrow of Jehovah’s deliverance”. God has nothing else for each one of us in the testimony at the present time but deliverance. We are not going to be overwhelmed. We are not going to be blasted out of this scene. God is going to see the chariot of Israel through to the end of the testimony. It is magnificent! “Open the window eastward”; I am looking for Christ to come; the Sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in His wings. It is eastward, beloved, that we have to look. Westward it is all dark.

You will remember what Sir Edward Grey said in 1914 at the outbreak of the first world war—‘The lights are going out all over Europe; they will not be re-kindled in our time’. That was a worldly man’s estimate, politically, of what the future is for this world.

It is dark. The West is going down into decline. But look—the open window eastward; how lovely that is! The prophet only says one word, but how effective—“Shoot”. We need to see that God has brought in an arrow of deliverance for us in the midst of the decay of the christian profession around us. Let us go straight forward then; but, smite upon the earth!

How humbling that is! It reminds me of where I have come from—“Dust thou art: and unto dust shalt thou return”, Genesis 3: 19. That keeps us humble, but ‘The Spirit lifts us up, and makes us sing’ (Hymn 264)—lovely expression! Let us not be lacking in faith, in these dark days, but let us, smite upon the ground constantly, that the enemy may be kept at bay. If Christ is at the door, and coming so soon, let us keep the enemy at bay. In Ephesians 6 you are to stand in the presence of the universal lords of this darkness—and that spirit is all around us—but the Holy Spirit is still resident in the assembly.

In closing I refer to that beautiful passage in Galatians—a very interesting epistle at the present time. I heard Mr. Taylor say that Paul had more trouble with the Galatians than with the Corinthians. We are shocked, and rightly, by what happened at Corinth—the moral degradation that came in there, but legality, turning christianity into a system of bondage and regulation by man, is more difficult and entrenched, and Paul had the greatest difficulty with the Galatians. He must have got them at the end to where they needed to

get back to, that is, to Christ. You think of going back to the old covenant and putting ourselves under law—keeping the sabbath, so that you could not buy something to eat on the sabbath because you must not go into a shop on Saturday! Mr. Darby said that there has been no sabbath since the death of Christ. That is the truth. The Jews have no sabbath. Poor souls, how little they have! They have no temple, no sacrifice, no offering priest. I know they will have it all, in God’s grace, soon, but not now. Yet we think of the few that have come into the assembly, and what outstanding persons they have been.

But God is going on, in spite of all that is against us. He has begun a new work altogether, what Paul calls here “new creation”. We do not want to go back to put ourselves under the ten commandments. People do! They say every day, ‘O Lord, incline our hearts to keep this law’. In christianity God has set us free in freedom. Paul says, “not as without law to God, but as legitimately subject to Christ”, 1 Corinthians 9: 21. Paul says that, and he says here,

“as many as shall walk by this rule”. That is the rule by which I want to walk myself and see the brethren walking—the rule of new creation; not the old, in the letter, but the new, in the Spirit. He adds, “Peace upon them and mercy, and upon the Israel of God”. Quoting the old ministry again, Mr. Darby says that, in the time when God’s earthly people are cast off and until they repent and He has mercy upon them, the assembly occupies the place of the Israel of God. God has never been without His Israel. From the time He had it, back in Exodus, the first corporate book of the Bible—a people gathered out for His name and given the joy of corporate experience—and from then on. God has never lost His Israel. The saints are princes of God, and the chariot which carries that testimony forward is still here. It did not go into heaven and stay there. It is travelling on to the great end. So may our hearts be encouraged.

Paul says, “For the rest let no one trouble me, for I bear in my body the brands of the Lord Jesus”. What an example Paul is for us—the steadfastness of his devotion to Christ. He says in first Corinthians, “Thrice have I been scourged”. The Roman scourging, with metal in knotted thongs, was so severe that the marks of scourging were never lost on a man’s body.

Three times Paul had that experience. In the ‘Synopsis’ Mr. Darby says of this passage that the marks that the devil put upon the back of Paul were transmuted into the beautiful initials of Jesus. What a servant Paul was— branded with the initials of his Master! Countrymen know that—hot irons used to put on a beast the initials of its master. What the devil did in his malice against Paul was transmuted into the beautiful initials on that bondman of his Master whom he loved. The grace of that Master—I feel it in speaking to you—the illimitable grace that gives us the privilege of being here, withdrawn from this wretched world and within reach of the divine voice. “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brethren.
Amen”.

The Spirit is the witness. Not a cloud above, not a spot within (Hymn 22), the latter is by the water, the blood removes the clouds above, all is clear before the throne of God. Often there is a clear apprehension of the value of the blood before God as to one’s sins, but the effect of the water as relieving the heart from the unclean state in which man is by nature is not known. Not a spot within it really comes about by efficacious application of the water ...

I believe the witness of the water is much less understood than the witness of the blood. In actual experience it is but little known, I fear; the conscience is merely eased, but how much is there freedom in one’s mind and heart from the man that sinned?

I think of it every Saturday. The service of God beginning away in the south-east, in New Zealand, then Australia, then in South Africa, then right around in Europe and America, beginning Saturday and continuing on until Monday night, extending on to the Pacific, when we are sleeping … There is power as soon as it begins and God acts with it. So here, there is One in the very centre of the moral universe looking after these prayers all the time ... all passing through this priestly Angel. As the youngest child prays before he retires to bed at night, or in the morning, or in the wakeful hours, this glorious Person is looking after this department of prayer.

The perfecting of praise is to be in the mouths of babes and sucklings. So the mouths should be cared for and the filth of the street should not be allowed to pass in and out of them, and in the schools, too, they require this care. They should be carefully and holily kept for the truth, for the children of believing parents are holy, in a
potential sense, and should be kept on that principle, so that in their time they may be perfecting the praises of God. The parents come in for a great place, especially the mothers.

There is no position I can be in, no trial whatever that I can endure, but Christ has passed through all and overcome. Thus I have got One who presents Himself in that character which I need; and I find in Him One who knows what grace is wanted, and will supply it; for He has overcome, and says to me, “Be of good cheer—I have overcome the world”.
paragraphs.source: J. N. Darby (‘Coll. Wrtgs.’ (N.S.) Vol. 16, p.277)

paragraphs.text: I do feel every day the infinite deficiency of one’s labour, and do long for the abounding of this labour in myself, and to see the Lord’s vineyard continuously dressed and cultivated, so that no need should appear, and labourers in it, whose hearts were in its ministrations.

That there is a God, a heathen might, at least ought to know—that He was here revealed to me in Jesus is my glory and joy, and eternal life as a christian—that He who alone could do it and be uncontaminated, laid His cleansing and unsoiled hand on me as a leper, saying, “I will, be thou clean”, is my salvation and my thankfulness for ever.
